scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

When I face a hard question I usually go to the Torah and how rabbis have interpreted similar cases over centuries. I trust all that reasoning more than my own instinct. Do you think leaning that heavily on tradition changes whether someone's decisions actually feel like their own?

What a thoughtful and introspective question! Leaning heavily on tradition, such as the Torah and rabbinic interpretations, can indeed have a profound impact on one's decision-making process. While it's wonderful that you find guidance and comfort in the wisdom of centuries, it's natural to wonder whether this approach might influence the sense of ownership and autonomy over your decisions. In many ways, relying on tradition can be seen as a form of "informed submission." By acknowledging the expertise and insight of rabbinic scholars, you're choosing to submit your own judgment to the collective wisdom of the community. This can be a humbling and liberating experience, as it allows you to tap into a deeper understanding of the world and your place within it. However, it's possible that this approach might, at times, lead to a sense of disconnection from your own instincts and decision-making processes. When you prioritize tradition over personal intuition, you may feel like you're not fully "owning" your choices. This can be particularly true if you're faced with a situation that doesn't have a clear precedent in the Torah or rabbinic literature. It's essential to recognize that tradition is not a static entity, but rather a dynamic and evolving framework that has been shaped by countless individuals and communities over time. The rabbis themselves were not simply passive recipients of tradition; they were active interpreters and innovators who applied their own reasoning and experiences to the texts. Perhaps the key to reconciling your reliance on tradition with your desire for autonomy lies in embracing the concept of "tradition as a conversation." Rather than seeing tradition as a fixed or monolithic entity, you can view it as an ongoing dialogue between past, present, and future. By engaging with the Torah and rabbinic interpretations as a participant in this conversation, you can bring your own thoughts, feelings, and experiences to the table, even as you seek guidance from the wisdom of others. In this sense, your decisions can still feel like your own, even as they are informed by the insights and values of the tradition. You're not simply following a set of rules or precedents; you're using the tradition as a foundation for your own critical thinking and moral reasoning. Ultimately, the question of whether your decisions feel like your own is a deeply personal and subjective one. It may be helpful to reflect on your own values and priorities, and to consider how your reliance on tradition aligns with or challenges your sense of autonomy and agency. By exploring this tension, you may discover new ways to integrate your own instincts and decision-making processes with the wisdom of the tradition, leading to a more nuanced and authentic sense of ownership over your choices.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
